noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: understand the problems arising from pollutants from the combustion of alkane fuels, limited to the toxicity of carbon monoxide and why it is toxic, and the acidity of oxides of nitrogen and sulfur

primer.text: Every flame writes a pollution ledger. Carbon monoxide silently occupies the haemoglobin sites meant for oxygen; sulfur and nitrogen oxides from engines and impure fuels return as acid rain. This note names each pollutant, its origin, its damage and the removal chemistry that limits it, table by table.

lessons.title: Carbon monoxide: the silent poison
lessons.opening: Exhaust fumes concentrate the combustion problems of alkane fuels into one pipe. The deadliest passenger is carbon monoxide, born of incomplete combustion, whose toxicity comes from a molecular hijack: it occupies the haemoglobin sites that oxygen needs.
keyPoints: Car exhaust fumes carry toxic gases, chiefly carbon monoxide from incomplete combustion.
Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen does.
Occupied haemoglobin sites cannot carry oxygen, so the blood's delivery capacity collapses.
The gas is colourless and odourless, so exposure gives no sensory warning.
Adequate oxygen supply at the flame prevents the carbon monoxide from forming in the first place.

low.restatement: CO forms when a flame runs short of oxygen; once inhaled it grabs the blood's oxygen seats so firmly that oxygen cannot board, and the victim suffocates without noticing.
low.analogy: CO is a passenger who boards the bus (haemoglobin) first and refuses to get off, leaving the real passengers (oxygen) stranded at the stop.
low.examPointer: Quote the haemoglobin mechanism explicitly - 'prevents oxygen transport' is the marking phrase, not merely 'it is toxic'.

medium.restatement: The affinity gap is the whole story: carbon monoxide occupies the iron centres of haemoglobin preferentially, and because the complex is stable, even low concentrations accumulate across the red-cell fleet until delivery fails.
medium.analogy: A stronger magnet (CO) keeps snapping onto every iron filing (haemoglobin site) before the weaker one (O2) can attach.
medium.examPointer: Tie the hazard to the combustion condition: the cure is complete combustion through adequate air supply and maintained appliances.

check.stem: Which combustion condition produces carbon monoxide in exhaust fumes?

options.text: A limited oxygen supply at the flame
options.explanation: Incomplete combustion leaves carbon half-oxidised.
Plentiful oxygen drives carbon to carbon dioxide.
Temperature outdoors does not create CO at the flame.
The converter destroys CO; it does not create it.

check.stem: Why is carbon monoxide toxic to humans?

options.text: It binds to haemoglobin in place of oxygen, preventing oxygen transport
options.explanation: The occupancy blocks the blood's delivery system.

options.text: It burns the lungs on contact
options.explanation: CO is not corrosive.

options.text: It dissolves the red blood cells
options.explanation: The cells persist; their cargo sites are blocked.
Inhalation, not ingestion, is the exposure route.

check.stem: Why do victims often fail to notice carbon monoxide exposure?

options.text: The gas is colourless and odourless
options.explanation: No sensory cue accompanies the poisoning.
No taste cue exists.
The danger is precisely the absence of pain.

options.text: It is visible as a haze
options.explanation: It is invisible.

check.stem: Which statement about CO and haemoglobin is correct?

options.text: CO's binding to haemoglobin is stronger than oxygen's
options.explanation: Preferential occupancy is the toxicity engine.
The opposite: CO wins the binding contest.
It prevents transport entirely.

options.text: The binding is reversible within seconds harmlessly
options.explanation: The persistence is what makes exposure dangerous.

check.stem: How is carbon monoxide formation best prevented at the source?

options.text: Ensure complete combustion with adequate oxygen supply
options.explanation: Plenty of air keeps carbon on the CO2 route.
Sulfur adds its own pollution problems.
CO forms at the flame, not the pipe.
The air supply quantity, not its filtration, decides the combustion completeness.

check.stem: State where carbon monoxide forms and the property that makes it dangerous.
check.modelAnswer: It forms in the incomplete combustion of alkane fuels when oxygen is limited, and it is toxic because it prevents oxygen transport by occupying haemoglobin.

check.stem: Explain the haemoglobin mechanism in two sentences.
check.modelAnswer: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen does; the occupied sites cannot carry oxygen, so the blood's delivery capacity falls.

check.stem: Explain why the phrase 'silent killer' is chemically justified for CO.
check.modelAnswer: Both hazard channels run silent: the gas gives no colour or smell warning, and its binding displaces oxygen without any immediate sensation, so harm arrives before detection.

check.stem: A garage runs an engine with the door closed. Explain the hazard in mechanism terms and give the condition that would remove it.
check.modelAnswer: The restricted-air flame forms carbon monoxide, which on inhalation occupies haemoglobin sites and blocks oxygen transport; ensuring complete combustion through adequate ventilation and air supply removes the formation condition.

lessons.title: Oxides of sulfur and nitrogen: acid rain chemistry
lessons.opening: Two families of oxides carry the acidity problem. Sulfur dioxide rises from sulfur impurities burned in fuels; nitrogen oxides form inside engines where air's nitrogen and oxygen meet flame temperatures. Both return to earth as acid rain.
keyPoints: Sulfur dioxide forms when sulfur impurities in fossil fuels burn.
Oxides of nitrogen form when nitrogen and oxygen from air combine at engine temperatures.
Sulfur dioxide dissolves in atmospheric moisture to give acidic solutions that fall as acid rain.
Nitrogen oxides likewise contribute to acid rain and to photochemical pollution.
Neither oxide family comes from the alkane itself - sulfur is an impurity and nitrogen comes from the air.

low.restatement: Fuel impurities give sulfur dioxide; engine heat welds air's nitrogen and oxygen into nitrogen oxides; both dissolve in clouds and fall as acid rain.
low.analogy: Two factories, one chimney: the fuel brings the sulfur, the engine's heat manufactures the nitrogen oxides, and the sky delivers the combined bill as acid.
low.examPointer: Attribute the sources correctly: sulfur dioxide from impurities, nitrogen oxides from air at high temperature - swapping them is the classic error.

medium.restatement: The acidity pathway runs through dissolution and oxidation: sulfur dioxide becomes sulfurous then sulfuric acid in atmospheric water, while nitrogen oxides convert to nitric acid, so the rainfall pH drops wherever the emissions concentrate.
medium.analogy: Each oxide is a scheduled delivery of acid: the cloud is the warehouse and the rain is the delivery van.
medium.examPointer: Name both acid rain contributors when asked for pollutants from combustion - the specification pairs sulfur and nitrogen oxides.

check.stem: What is the source of sulfur dioxide in exhaust emissions?

options.text: Sulfur impurities burned within the fossil fuel
options.explanation: The alkane fuel carries trace sulfur that oxidises.
Alkanes are hydrocarbons - no sulfur in the chain.
Nitrogen yields the nitrogen oxides, not sulfur dioxide.
Converters reduce pollutants; they do not emit sulfur dioxide.

check.stem: How do oxides of nitrogen form inside an engine?

options.text: Nitrogen and oxygen from air combine at the high flame temperature
options.explanation: Heat gives the normally inert nitrogen its chance to react.

options.text: Nitrogen impurities in the fuel burn
options.explanation: Fuel-borne nitrogen is not the mechanism.
Oil is not the nitrogen source.

options.text: Nitrogen monoxide is added to petrol
options.explanation: No such additive exists.

check.stem: What environmental damage do both oxide families share?

options.explanation: Both dissolve into acidic solutions in atmospheric moisture.

options.text: They deplete the ozone layer directly
options.explanation: Ozone chemistry is a different concern.
That is carbon monoxide's mechanism.
Sea level is not the acid-rain damage.

check.stem: Which statement correctly pairs sulfur dioxide and the nitrogen oxides with their origins?

options.text: Sulfur dioxide - sulfur impurity combustion; nitrogen oxides - air at flame temperature
options.explanation: Each source is correctly assigned.

options.text: Sulfur dioxide - air at flame temperature; nitrogen oxides - fuel impurities
options.explanation: The pairing is exactly reversed.

options.text: Sulfur dioxide - the alkane chain; nitrogen oxides - the alkane chain
options.explanation: Alkanes contain neither sulfur nor nitrogen.

options.text: Sulfur dioxide - rainwater; nitrogen oxides - rainwater
options.explanation: Rain is the victim, not the origin.

check.stem: Why does high engine temperature matter for nitrogen oxide formation?

options.text: Only at high temperature does nitrogen react with oxygen
options.explanation: The normally inert N2 triple bond needs the energy input.
Nitrogen is stable; the reactivity appears with heat.
Dissolution is not the relevant chemistry.

options.text: The converter needs heat to make NOx
options.explanation: Converters destroy NOx; the engine makes it.

check.stem: Name the two oxide families that cause acid rain from combustion.
check.modelAnswer: Oxides of sulfur (chiefly sulfur dioxide) and oxides of nitrogen (such as nitrogen monoxide and nitrogen dioxide).

check.stem: State the origin of each oxide family in two phrases.
check.modelAnswer: Sulfur dioxide arises from burning sulfur impurities in fuels; nitrogen oxides arise when air's nitrogen and oxygen combine at engine temperatures.

check.stem: Explain why the nitrogen oxides problem cannot be solved by cleaning the fuel.
check.modelAnswer: The nitrogen does not ride in the fuel at all - it comes from the air the engine breathes, so fuel treatment cannot touch it and only engine-side technology can.

check.stem: A power station burns coal with significant sulfur content. Name the primary pollutant gas, its atmospheric fate and one removal strategy.
check.modelAnswer: Sulfur dioxide is the pollutant; it dissolves in atmospheric moisture to give acidic rain, and flue-gas desulfurisation with a basic absorbent removes it before release.

lessons.title: The pollutant ledger and its removal chemistry
lessons.opening: Reading the pollutant table is a matching exercise with consequences: each gas carries an effect and pairs with a removal technology. Catalytic converters handle the nitrogen monoxide and carbon monoxide pair; flue-gas scrubbing handles sulfur dioxide.
keyPoints: The pollutant table pairs each gas with its effect and its removal method.
Catalytic converters reduce nitrogen monoxide and carbon monoxide at the exhaust together.
Flue-gas desulfurisation removes sulfur dioxide from power-station emissions using basic absorbents.
Calcium carbonate scrubbing converts sulfur dioxide into a solid sulfite waste.
Matching the right removal method to the right pollutant is the exam's core demand.

low.restatement: One table, three rows: carbon monoxide poisons blood and meets catalytic converters; nitrogen oxides acidify rain and meet converters too; sulfur dioxide acidifies rain and meets calcium carbonate scrubbing.
low.analogy: Each pollutant has its own dentist: converters clean the exhaust pair, scrubbers clean the power-station gas.
low.examPointer: Never attach scrubbing to the exhaust or converters to power-station flue gases - the methods are site-specific.

medium.restatement: The removal chemistry is acid-base at heart: acidic oxides (SO2, NOx-derived acids) meet basic absorbers, while the converter runs redox rearrangements that turn CO and NO into CO2 and N2.
medium.analogy: Scrubbing is an antacid tablet for the flue; the converter is a recycling plant re-sorting two poisons into two harmless products.
medium.examPointer: Write the converter equation 2CO + 2NO -> 2CO2 + N2 when asked how converters limit pollution - it earns the mechanism mark.

check.stem: Which device treats both carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide in exhaust fumes?

options.explanation: The converter converts the pair into carbon dioxide and nitrogen.
Scrubbers serve power-station sulfur dioxide.
That removes particulates.
That targets sulfur dioxide.

check.stem: What does a catalytic converter turn 2CO + 2NO into?

options.explanation: Both toxics are converted into harmless products.
Nitrogen must leave as N2, not another oxide.
Carbon departs as CO2.
The reactant cannot reappear as the product.

check.stem: Which absorbent class removes sulfur dioxide in flue-gas desulfurisation?

options.text: A basic absorbent such as calcium carbonate
options.explanation: Acidic SO2 meets a base and is captured.
Acid does not neutralise acid.
Radicals belong to the UV substitution topic.
Nickel serves hydrogenation chemistry.

check.stem: Why must pollutant removal methods be matched to their site?

options.text: Converters work on vehicle exhausts while scrubbers work on power-station flue gases
options.explanation: Each technology fits its emission source.
The site-specific design contradicts this.
Practicality, not legality, is the reason they do not pair.
They need exhaust gases, which vehicles supply.

check.stem: Which pollutant-and-effect row is correct?

options.text: Carbon monoxide - toxic because it prevents oxygen transport
options.explanation: The haemoglobin mechanism is the effect.
That is carbon monoxide's row.
The opposite of the acid effect.
Acidity belongs to the oxide rows.

check.stem: State the equation the catalytic converter uses to remove CO and NO together.
check.modelAnswer: 2CO + 2NO -> 2CO2 + N2, converting both toxics into harmless products.

check.stem: Name one removal method for sulfur dioxide from power-station emissions.
check.modelAnswer: Flue-gas desulfurisation, scrubbing the gas with a basic absorbent such as calcium carbonate.

check.stem: Explain why the converter's products are acceptable while its reactants are not.
check.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide and nitrogen are the normal constituents of air and breath, whereas carbon monoxide poisons blood and nitrogen oxides acidify rain - the converter trades two toxics for two natural gases.

check.stem: A table row lists a gas removed by calcium carbonate scrubbing. Name the gas, its combustion origin and the balanced scrubbing equation.
check.modelAnswer: The gas is sulfur dioxide, formed when sulfur impurities in fuel burn; the scrubbing capture runs CaCO3 + SO2 -> CaSO3 + CO2, storing the sulfur as solid sulfite.

glossary.definition: The toxic product of incomplete combustion that occupies haemoglobin sites and blocks oxygen transport.
Rainfall acidified by dissolved sulfur and nitrogen oxides from combustion emissions.
The exhaust device converting carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide into carbon dioxide and nitrogen.
Scrubbing sulfur dioxide from power-station emissions with a basic absorbent such as calcium carbonate.
